On Saturday, May 13, 2017 at 7:03:26 PM UTC+2, Nick Matzke wrote:

> Hi Marie Claire, sorry for the slow reply...
>
> Briefly,
>
> 1. The error message was accurate.  Your areas-adjacency file was removing states from the states space (meaning, removing ranges from the list of ranges), and one of the removed ranges was found in one of your living species.  If a living species has a range that is disallowed, this causes the error you got.
>
> 2. As noted in various places, the areas_adjacency file can only do very simple forms of area adjacency (e.g., Hawaiian islands, max_range_size=2, allow only the closest pairs of islands to form ranges).
>
> 3. The alternative is to manually specify your states_list.  I include complete code for doing this below, and in a revised version of your script.  I have now also put the code here:
>
> Manual modification of states_list (list of geographic ranges, a.k.a. the list of states in the state space)
> http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#manual_modify_states
>
> Re-using the manually modified of states_list
> http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#reuse_modified_states
>
> Manually modify the states list in time-stratified analyses
> http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#modified_states_stratified
>
>
> 3.5. The code:
>
> ===========
> #######################################################
> # START MANUAL MODIFICATION OF STATES LIST
> # Manually modify the list of states (geographic ranges)
> # to disallow some ranges that are disjunct
> # (allow more complex scenarios than the area-adjacency file)
> #######################################################
>
> #######################################################
> # NOTE! "areas" and "states/ranges" are DIFFERENT THINGS
> # NOTHING WILL MAKE SENSE UNLESS you understand that a
> # STATE/RANGE is made up of some number of areas.
> #
> # E.g.: 2 areas (A,B) equals
> # 4 states/geographic ranges (null, A, B, AB)
> #######################################################
>
> # Get your states list (assuming, say, 4-area analysis, with max. rangesize=4)
> max_range_size = 4
> areas = getareas_from_tipranges_object(tipranges)
> #areas = c("A", "B", "C", "D")
>
> # This is the list of states/ranges, where each state/range
> # is a list of areas, counting from 0
> states_list_0based = rcpp_areas_list_to_states_list(areas=areas, maxareas=max_range_size, include_null_range=TRUE)
>
> # How many states/ranges, by default: 163
> length(states_list_0based)
>
> # Make the list of ranges
> ranges_list = NULL
> for (i in 1:length(states_list_0based))
>     {
>     if ( (length(states_list_0based[[i]]) == 1) && (is.na <http://is.na>(states_list_0based[[i]])) )
>         {
>         tmprange = "_"
>         } else {
>         tmprange = paste(areas[states_list_0based[[i]]+1], collapse="")
>         }
>     ranges_list = c(ranges_list, tmprange)
>     }
>
> # Look at the ranges list
> ranges_list
>
> # How many states/ranges, by default: 163
> length(ranges_list)
>
> # Let's remove some non-adjacent ranges
> nonadjacent=c("AC","AD","AE","AF","AG","AH","BE","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")
> keepTF = ranges_list %in% nonadjacent == FALSE
>
> ranges_list_NEW = ranges_list[keepTF]
> length(ranges_list_NEW)     # now 148
>
> states_list_0based_NEW = states_list_0based[keepTF]
> length(states_list_0based_NEW)     # now 148
>
> # INPUT the NEW states list into the BioGeoBEARS_run_object
> BioGeoBEARS_run_object$states_list = states_list_0based_NEW
>
> #######################################################
> # END MANUAL MODIFICATION OF THE STATES LIST
> #######################################################
> ===========
>
>
>
> 4. Your areas_adjacency file looked like it had 8 time slices, but they were all identical in terms of adjacency.  You had no timeperiods file, so only the first areas_adjacency matrix was being looked at.
>
> Here, I show how to do different manual states lists in different time periods, if that was your goal:
>
> Manually modify the states list in time-stratified analyses
> http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#modified_states_stratified
>
>
> 5. I attach a revised script for your analysis, with your modified states_list, for a non-time stratified analysis.
>
> 5.5. I also attach a script showing how the time-stratified version would work (although you would have to manually modify this further to produce *different* area adjacencies in different time-slices.
>
>
>
> 6. Also -- with your manual modifications to the states_list, the DIVALIKE model produces errors.  This is probably because you eliminated some two-area ranges that the DIVALIKE model thinks should be used to explain tips in different areas.  There may be a way to get it working (probably higher starting rates for d and e), but I didn't explore it.
>
>
> 7. It is worth thinking about the logic of, say, allowing range ABC, but disallowing the disjunct range AC.  ABC can transform to AC just by local extirpation in B.  To make this a plausible argument, one would have to say something like "range ABC can be maintained by a species for a long period of time because of high gene flow between areas in a high-dispersing species", whereas "for AC, the distance between A and C is so great that it is not expected that gene flow could be maintained for any measurable length of time (relative to a timescale of millions of years, that is), so this range is not considered a plausible state in the state space".  If a decent argument was provided based on biology, perhaps this is a reasonable idea, but it shouldn't be blindly assumed.
>
> A really good model would include something about how "ability to maintain gene flow" is a trait that itself evolves on the tree, but this would be a model much more complex than anything in BioGeoBEARS.  Another model would have a forced ultrahigh rate on range AC splitting to form species in areas A and C.  This would be more of an SSE model, but these are computationally very slow.
>
> Speaking for myself, my gut instinct is that in most cases, it is better to use area adjacency to modify the state space only in the simplest hypotheses, and otherwise use a geographical distance matrix to influence/represent changes in dispersal probability between regions that are far apart from each other.  This will tend to lower the probability of species expanding their ranges across highly disjunct ranges, which is usually all people are trying to do anyway.
>
> Cheers,
> Nick

Hi -- the reason that DIVALIKE run is taking so long is that you are running a Maximum Likelihood analysis, but the LnL (the log of the likelihood) is coming up as NaN.  So nothing is optimizing, and it may run forever for all I know.  Surely you have seen how the LnL is supposed to increase (becomes less negative) in the runs that work??

Before I look at details, **important** point here:

The goal with BioGeoBEARS, or any analysis, not to "get it to run".  The real goal is to understand what you are doing!!!!!  The current script has this for each model:

===================
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[1]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[2]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[3]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[4]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[5]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[6]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[7]] = states_list_0based_NEW
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$lists_of_states_lists_0based[[8]] = states_list_0based_NEW
===================

...this means you are time-stratifying the analysis, but each timeperiod has an identical list of states!  So, there is no reason to time-stratify.

However, you get the same error with a non-time stratified analysis (lnL=-1e50 is equivalent to lnL=NaN), if the states_list is constrained.

OK, looking at your run:

1. The problem seems to be caused by the interaction between your user-constrained states_list and the DIVALIKE model. Between tips 2 and 3 (AB and BDE, tiplabels 1767 and 2359), the analysis can find no scenario that gives these tip data a nonzero probability at their common ancestor node. DEC allows subset-sympatry as well as vicariance, so it is more flexible, but DIVALIKE is vicariance-only.  This produces a NaN in the likelihood, which then produces a LnL=-1e50 under some settings.

This would be fine if it happened somewhere in the middle of the chain -- sometimes extreme parameter values get tried and result in NaN likelihoods, these are converted to -1e50 and the analysis says "Wow, that was a horrible guess at parameter values, let's try something else."  But, if even your starting parameters produce NaN, probably you've got an overly-constrained states lists.

2. I fiddled with your list of disallowed ranges:

This is what failed:
nonadjacent=c("AC","AD","AE","AF","AG","AH","BE","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")

This, however, worked:
nonadjacent=c("AF","AG","AH","BG","BH","CG","CH","DF","DG","DH","EH")

...however, including AD, BE, etc. as disallowed ranges caused crashes again. So, these are crucial intermediate states for explaining sister species like (AB, BDE), under the DIVALIKE model.

3.  HAVE A SERIOUS THINK ABOUT WHY YOU ARE CONSTRAINING ALLOWED RANGES AT ALL!  For example, you have a tip range of BDE.  All that is required to turn BDE into BE is an "e" event, loss of D.  So, how can BE really be considered an impossible range?  You have allowed everything up to ranges with a size of 4 areas, so eliminating a few 2-area ranges is a bit odd.

4. I have now updated the code so that an explicit error message is produced if the initial lnL calculation fails, and the run is stopped,.  Update from GitHub to get this fix.

5. On the other issues, you should really walk before you run!  In all things, the first steps are:

5a. Take a deep breath and review your decisions...does what your script is doing make sense?

5b. Do the same for whatever a reviewer says...reviewers often suggest things because they are mildly curious, that might make no difference.

6. "I have also tried o search for nay published paper using multiple Beast trees for the Biogeo analyses. but not seen any. Do you know of any such paper."

One of them is Wood, Matzke et al. 2012, Systematic Biology -- this was before BioGeoBEARS, but it ran Lagrange on a bunch of trees.  IMHO the effort-to-reward ratio was marginal in that case, but like I say here, it will all depend on how variable the BEAST trees are compared to the MCC tree: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/M8zw8Kidseo

Cheers,
Nick

Hi -- R has a large number of functions that do optimization (of likelihood or any other function that returns an objective that can be maximized or minimized).  There is a little world of such optimizers and math-type-people who construct them.

BioGeoBEARS allows 3 options:

optim (from default R)
optimx (from optimx R package)
GenSA (from GenSA R package)

...specifically, within each of these, a sub-algorithm is chosen that optimizes parameters within bounds (one of these is called L-BGFS-B, which if you google it you will see is an algorithm found in all sorts of implementations in various computer languages.

Each of these has a "stopping rule", which is something like "if the objective fails to improve by 0.00001 after x steps, then stop".  Sometimes the criterion is about the inferred slope of the objective (which will be 0 at the peak).  Usually there is an obscure way to change the default, but it is not trivial and requires burrowing into the original package (and sometimes the FORTRAN or C++ code underneath the R package).

Each optimizer returns a result which contains the maximized objective value, the parameters that produced this value, and some information on the search.  BioGeoBEARS just includes this whole output in the results object; to interpret it, you have to study the help for the original optimizer functions.

In general, speed works like this:

>From faster to slower:
=============================
optimx with $speedup=TRUE
(the speedup=TRUE setting in BioGeoBEARS sets limits on the maximum number of iterations to search through)

optimx with $speedup=FALSE

optim

GenSA
=============================

In general, accuracy (meaning avoiding optimization failure, claiming a Max. Likelihood result that is a local optimum rather than the actual Maximum of the Likelihood) seems to work like this:
GenSA > optimx with $speedup=FALSE > optimx with $speedup=TRUE > optim

...but for most basic problems they all return the same thing.  The only place I've seen this trend matter in any reliable way is (1) very complex models (base models +x +traits etc.) or (2) weird cases with tiny datasets and 2 optima.

Therefore, if you have a particularly complex model, or just are worried, use GenSA (but it may take 2-10 times as long).

Regardless, no optimizer is perfect, these are just hill-climbing algorithms of various sorts.  Advice:

ML optimization routines and their pitfalls
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#ML_optimx

In addition to the optimizer, the run time will be influenced by many other things:

More areas = more states/ranges = slower matrix exponentiation = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
More free parameters = bigger parameter space to search through = slower overall run
Slower/older computer = slower likelihood calculation = slower overall run
Fewer cores / not using the multiple cores (R in Mac Terminal can do multicores, R.app cannot) = slower overall run

Cheers,
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- that seems odd, unless maybe it's a time-stratified analysis where multicore isn't as helpful?

Nothing in the code about the parallel-processing stuff has changed in a long time, either before or after the GitHub setup.  You'll have to experiment to see if you can improve behavior:

1. Try re-installing with explicit byte-compilation (I think this happens automatically anyway, but you can try it)

2. Run your script from the Terminal (not through a GUI like R.app or RStudio), e.g.:

Rscript myScript_v1.R

or on some systems:

Rscript myScript_v1.R | tee screenoutput_v1.txt &

(the tee saves the screenoutput to a text file, which can be handy)

3. They may have changed something about parallel or snow work (and these function somewhat differently between different operating systems), you might try running with just one of these two commands:

library(parallel)
...or...
library(snow)

...in your script. (It may be that both are required on your OS)

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- you can do this, just make sure you copy/save and write down all the parameters that have been printed to screen.  Then you will have to

1. manually enter the best-guess parameters into the "init" and "est" fields of the params_table:

# if the maximum likelihood estimate said parameter "d" was 0.123

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["d","init"] = 0.123
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["d","est"] = 0.123

2. Then, run the likelihood calculation one more time to produce ancestral states at that ML estimate:

res = bears_optim_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object=BioGeoBEARS_run_object, skip_optim=TRUE, skip_optim_option="return_all")

The object "res" will now have the same stuff it would have if the ML run had finished on its own.

Cheers,
Nick
